title: Good Quantum Locally Testable Codes from Lossless Cubical Complexes
authors: Itay Cohen, Itai Leigh, Assaf Reiner, Amnon Ta-Shma, Elad Tzalik
abstract: Sipser and Spielman constructed LDPC codes from either bipartite \emph{spectral} expanders or one-sided \emph{lossless} expanders. In higher dimensions, \emph{spectral} expansion similarly played a central role in the constructions of asymptotically good classical LTCs and qLDPC codes by Dinur, Evra, Livne, Lubotzky, and Mozes and by Panteleev and Kalachev. Alternatively, Lin and Hsieh constructed classical LTCs and qLDPC codes from two-dimensional \emph{lossless} cubical complexes.   In this work we develop the higher-dimensional \emph{lossless} approach. We do not construct the required high-dimensional lossless cubical complexes; rather, we investigate what their existence would imply. We associate with a high-dimensional cubical complex a \emph{level chain complex}, whose chain groups are supported on the level sets of the Boolean cube rather than on its cells. Our main technical contribution is a clean local-to-global theorem for this structure: suitable one-dimensional lossless expansion in the directional graphs implies small-set coboundary expansion of the global level complex. As a consequence, sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes give rise to asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes. We expect the local-to-global principle developed here to have further applications.
summary: This paper develops a theoretical framework to construct quantum locally testable codes by analyzing the properties of high-dimensional lossless cubical complexes. It establishes a local-to-global principle that links directional expansion within these complexes to the existence of good quantum codes. This advances the understanding of how combinatorial geometry can guarantee robust quantum error correction.
main_problem: Developing asymptotically good Quantum Locally Testable Codes (qLTCs) using a higher-dimensional combinatorial approach based on lossless cubical complexes.
main_result: The existence of sufficiently imbalanced, two-sided lossless four-dimensional cubical complexes guarantees the existence of asymptotically good quantum locally testable codes.
method: The authors associate a high-dimensional cubical complex with a level chain complex and establish a local-to-global theorem linking directional lossless expansion to small-set coboundary expansion.
model_or_system: The model is quantum error correction, specifically constructing qLTCs. The mathematical framework involves high-dimensional lossless cubical complexes and their associated level chain complexes.
key_observables: Code parameters such as rate, distance, and the ability to achieve local testability soundness.
important_parameters: The dimension of the cubical complex (e.g., four-dimensional), the degree of imbalance, and the expansion properties (lossless expansion).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is investigating the implications of the existence of the required high-dimensional lossless cubical complexes, as explicit construction is not provided.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structure of complexes (e.g., left-right Cayley complex) and the application of algorithms like the Greedy Flipping Algorithm for bounding parameters.
paper_structure: The paper builds from classical LTCs to qLTCs, formalizing the structure via level chain complexes. It develops a local-to-global principle and then analyzes the resulting code parameters, including bounding distance and presenting a linear-time decoder.
why_interesting: The connection between high-dimensional combinatorial structures (lossless complexes) and the existence of robust quantum error-correcting codes provides a powerful, abstract tool for designing fault-tolerant quantum computation protocols.

Figure 4: The four vertex sets of a two-dimensional square complex, arranged by level. An initial set of vertices H1 is marked heavy (red) on level 1. In the layer below, only vertices that have many heavy parents are heavy. In the layer above, all upward neighbors of the heavy vertices are marked heavy. Terminal vertices (heavy vertices without heavy children) are enlarged. Red vertices shaped like diamonds, stars, and triangles have excess. The excess of the triangular vertex is accounted for by Same2, whereas the excess of the diamond shaped vertex is accounted for by Light2. The excess of the star shaped vertex is accounted for by both functions.
